section_name: Introduction — Why Rubrics Matter for PK-2
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Introduction: Why Rubrics Matter

In this fourth episode, we're talking about utilizing rubrics with writers who communicate in pictures, words, and/or early sentences. This includes those in the primary grades, those who are English language learners, and those with special needs.

Teaching writing isn't just about providing direct instruction; it's also about offering customized feedback. Students need this — they want this. They often run up to the teacher, showing her their writing, and asking, "Do you like it? Is this good? Am I done?"

Providing feedback via writer conferences is a huge component of growing writers. However, with one teacher and 20 plus students, we also need a kid-friendly assessment tool that THEY can use independently.

Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Limitations of Checklists

Attempting to meet this need, many teachers turn to checklists. After writing, students grab the checklist and evaluate their own work for the skills they were to include. They self assess each writing skill by circling thumbs up or down or checking a box — yes or no. For basic sentence-level skills, checklists CAN be helpful, especially when students are looking for specific marks or conventions.

However, a major limitation of a checklist is the difficulty in applying it to more abstract writing skills like whether it includes details, description, or goes in order. Without clear visual cues to look for, students often don't know how to assess those skills... so they opt to skip over them and just continue checking all the boxes.

A second limitation of checklists is that they don't indicate the quality of the writing skills. For example, two students might both check the box for having included a detailed picture... but one student communicated his idea in a single-color scribble while the other generated a colorful scene with recognizable objects. Even if the checklist includes more than 2 levels... checklists still don't offer the student guidance on HOW to improve his writing. He knows something is weak or missing, but the checklist doesn't indicate HOW to fix it or make it better. Consequently, the writer doesn't know what to do next.

section_name: Six Characteristics of a Strong Writing Rubric
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Rubric Advantages and Six Characteristics

A rubric, on the other hand, overcomes these weaknesses. It not only identifies the characteristics of a "good one", but honors the progress students make on their way to that goal. While a checklist is often a stopping point for students, a rubric reveals the tangible baby steps to take in order to improve his writing.

Let's look at 6 characteristics of a strong writing rubric:

1. Multiple Levels: An initial writing rubric has at least 3 levels — and in the primary, they usually begin with 4-5. These levels represent the wide variety of developmental stages, ensuring that every student feels valued regardless of where he is in his writing journey.

2. Explicit Criteria: Each level is defined by a list of writing skills it includes. These skills are communicated in simple language and minimal words. Young writers are young readers, so this assessment tool has to be kid-friendly and accessible.

3. Standards-Based: The rubric criteria is based on grade-level writing standards. And it includes more than just language foundations and concepts of print. It also assesses the expression and organization of ideas... regardless if the student wrote multiple sentences... or only provided a picture.

4. Visual Assets: Columns, graphics, and color visually represent the different levels and individual skills, making the rubric easily understandable.

5. Concrete Examples: An evolving writing sample shows the increasing expectations at each level. This interprets the criteria listed and reveals to students what that level looks like and sounds like.

Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Student-Generated Rubric

And one final characteristic (6)... AND likely the most important one... An instructional writing rubric is made WITH the students. It's not made by the teacher... and it's not found online. Although you can use examples as sources of inspiration for what to put on your rubric, the actual assessment tool must be made for... and WITH your students. This isn't a suggestion; this is best practice.

Research shows that students are more engaged and motivated when they help set their own academic goals and track their progress. By creating a writing rubric together, students become active participants in their learning and ultimately more independent in assessing and improving their own writing.

section_name: Instructional Rubrics Honor the Range of Writers
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Range of Writers and Instructional vs. Data Collection Rubrics

This begins with determining the range of writing abilities that your rubric has to account for. When I say "range of writers"... most teachers perk up and think "Oh yeah, I definitely have a WIDE range of writers!" And I'm not surprised to hear this. We've got first graders who know and write sentences in the same classroom with those who don't know all their sounds and letters yet. We've got second graders writing 6-8 sentences at the beginning of the year in the same room with peers struggling to compose a single thought with a capital and end mark.

This wide range of writers is EXACTLY why you WANT an instructional rubric. Rubrics represent the MANY different levels your writers are at. They HONOR that a piece of writing may NOT be at the goal or highest level yet, but that it's on the board... and on its way. An instructional rubric represents everyone in your class... your lowest... your varying middle level writers... and it will even CHALLENGE your highest to CONTINUE to improve. Again, this is one of the advantages of a rubric over say a checklist. Checklists are yes or no... you did it or didn't... But instructional rubrics represent the RANGE of writing abilities in a classroom.

Let me say that another way... an instructional rubric is made for A class... a single class. YOU make an instructional rubric WITH and FOR... YOUR students. Every class has strong writers... and weak writers. However, every section of that grade level does not necessarily have similar looking HIGHS and equally low LOWS.

Therefore we WON'T have the SAME INSTRUCTIONAL rubric in all of our classrooms. The first grade teachers are NOT creating a rubric to use AMONG ALL the first grade classrooms. Now, don't be confused. There ARE common rubrics that we all HAVE to use sometimes. BUT those are called DATA COLLECTION rubrics. Those are consistent, never changing rubrics used by all the teachers in a grade level to track and triangulate data in order to drive future instruction. These data collection rubrics DO have a place in our curriculum. However, those are complex and wordy and list ALL the writing skills students should be able to do by the END of the year. But we need an ADDITIONAL assessment tool... one that students can easily comprehend and start using at the BEGINNING of the year.

section_name: Building the Rubric — Teacher Prep Work
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Teacher Prep Work for Building the Rubric

Now that we have a common understanding of what a rubric IS and is NOT... let's transition into how to "make" one. Although we will build the rubric WITH the students, the teacher has a little prep work to do BEFORE that lesson.

Identify a recent writing that your students created independently. This should be a piece they wrote without any assistance from you. It wasn't shared writing, copied from the board, or dictated by you. If they drew a picture, it was all on their own. If they added letters or labels, it was all on their own. If they wrote sentences, it was all on their own. Analyzing THESE independent writing pieces will determine the WHOLE range of writing levels that you will need on YOUR instructional rubric.

Now, if you don't have any writing like this — or you did, but sent it home, no problem. Set aside a few minutes in the next couple of days to give students an opportunity to write about... their families... or a fun time at recess. Don't make it a challenging topic or one based on content knowledge. Just give them a relatable subject, some paper, and some time. Provide them with the writer tools they are most familiar with. Pre-K and Kindergarten might consider whether the paper should have lines on it. First and second grade teachers might consider whether there should be space for a picture or not. We don't want to omit a picture if that's how they predominantly communicate, but we also don't want them drawing with crayons simply because it's more fun than writing with a pencil.

section_name: Building the Rubric — Determining Levels and Criteria
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Determining Rubric Levels and Criteria

With a set of authentic writing from your class... sort it into 3 piles... High, Middle, Low. Now it's time to analyze them to determine the criteria for your rubric levels.

Start by studying 2-3 writing samples that you collected from your HIGHEST students. Look at the skills included, keeping in mind — Which ones have you TAUGHT this year? Consider the quality of the ideas conveyed in pictures and words. Look at the quantity of letters or sentences written. Analyze the accuracy of spacing, spelling & capitalization. Determine what each of these skills looks like in the writing done by your strongest writers... then itemize these skills within a bulleted list using simple kid-friendly words. This will become the criteria for your SECOND-to-highest level — we'll call it 4 star writing.

Now consider 1-2 skills that are currently missing... weak... or inconsistent within these HIGH-level student writings. What skill(s) would make these writings slightly better? List these additional skills — along with those from 4-star writing — to create the criteria for 5 star writing. Although this level IS better than your strongest writers, it gives them a goal to work toward.

Repeat the process using 2-3 writing samples that you collected from your WEAKEST writers. Analyze the quality of the picture, the quantity of letters or words, the accuracy of spacing & spelling. Again, detail these skills as they are depicted in the lowest writing samples. This will be the criteria for 1-star writing.

Now it's time to determine the middle levels. Read through several more writing samples that you collected from your average writers. Again, identify the ingredients that they have in common. This will include ALL of the skills listed in Level 1 but only a few of the skills listed in Level 4. This criteria represents 2 star writing. Repeat the process again. Using the skills listed in Level 2... up the ante slightly to describe 3-star writing.

section_name: Revising the Rubric Criteria Before Sharing with Students
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Revising the Rubric Before Sharing

You have now DRAFTED the criteria for your instructional writing rubric — but you'll want to review it and likely make some revisions before sharing it with students. These include:

- List only skills that you have taught or reviewed this year. Don't hold students accountable for skills you haven't introduced yet.
- Remove any references to negatives. Rubric criteria lists what writers ARE doing at that level, so don't describe what they DIDN'T include.
- Revise each skill to state it in as few words as possible. Remember, these are young READERS who we want to be able to use this rubric INDEPENDENTLY.
- Itemize each new ingredient within its own bullet. For example, rather than just listing "a detailed picture," reference the colors, the shapes, and the close-up details within individual bullets. I know we want capital letters at the beginning of sentences and punctuation at the end, but make those 2 separate items of criteria. Also, separate "spelling" expectations between word wall words and big words stretched out. We want students to be able to self-assess each skill individually... rather than looking for several things at once.
- Be sure that levels show a gradual progression — including only 2-3 new skills in the next level. We don't want students to feel like they have to make a major leap to move up the rubric. Increase the expectations incrementally, including only subtle differences between each level. You can always split criteria across 2 levels to slow down the progression even more.
- Consider how you will indicate what the new skills are in a level. One suggestion is to always note them at the top of the criteria and even indicate them with a different color font or marker.
- Although the picture is a key facet of writing in some grades, it may be a characteristic that eventually falls off of another grade level rubric. Rather than separating all the different picture criteria, the higher levels may combine them to de-emphasize them. It's a sign of growth and sophistication that a picture is no longer necessary after a certain point.

section_name: Introducing the Rubric to Students and Teaching How to Use It
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Introducing and Teaching the Rubric

With the initial rubric criteria developed and the number of levels determined, now it's time to create a set of writing samples that mirror the criteria per level. You'll want to generate these samples — not use actual student writing. No one wants to be the author of the lowest level on the Class rubric. Be sure that the samples are all on the same topic because we want students to appreciate the evolution of the same writing as it moves up the levels. When choosing the topic for these samples that you'll generate, be sure to select one students can relate to, but not a topic they would be writing about at any point this year. Think about places they would go when running errands with a parent — like the grocery store or a hardware store. Or things they know OF because they have seen it but don't actually DO themselves — like laundry or yard work. Any of these would be good topics to generate a set of parallel writing samples.

Once you've determined the leveled criteria for your rubric and created the sample pieces, it's time to introduce the rubric to your students. Your mini-lesson might open like this: "We are learning more and more about how to write well... and we are learning that there is A LOT you have to remember. BUT, instead of asking Mrs. Smekens if what you wrote is done... and if it's good... we are going to use a Class Writing Rubric. Say 'RUBRIC.' Good. A rubric lets US see how good our OWN writing is... AND what WE can do to make it EVEN better."

Now, point to a section of the wall where you've posted the title and the set of numbered stars. Emphasize that everyone is at different levels and working to improve. Start by showing the writing sample you created for Level 1. Read aloud the criteria for this level while pointing out the skills in the sample. Focus on the positive aspects of the writing, even for this lowest level. Don't mention what is missing or "bad" about the writing. Remember, these rubric levels are based on your students' writing skills. We don't want anyone thinking that he is a "bad" writer.

After reading aloud the criteria for Level 1 and posting the sample, repeat this process with the 2-star writing. Emphasize the additional skills in this next level and point out what they look like within the second example. Continue doing this until all levels are posted with their specific criteria and a writing sample.

section_name: Teaching Students How to Use the Rubric — Second Mini-Lesson
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Second Mini-Lesson: How to Use the Rubric

Now, knowing that a mini-lesson is only about 15 minutes, it's likely that this is about all you will get done. So, conclude the lesson identifying a DIFFERENT topic for students to write about... and encourage them to go for 5-star writing during writing time.

Although that first lesson introduced the rubric, it didn't teach students how to use it. In a second mini-lesson, teach students explicitly how the rubric helps them make their writing even better. Pull out a previous writing and walk up to the posted rubric. (It's important to put the rubric in a location where students can easily interact with it.) Model how you look at the different anchor papers posted on the rubric to determine which one LOOKS most like your writing. After focusing in on a single level, model how to read the corresponding criteria like a checklist.

- Put your finger on the first skill in the criteria and read it out loud.
- Use a magnifying glass or eyeglasses to look for evidence of this skill within your own writing... be a rubric detective.
- Be methodical in this process, looking carefully and closely in different places on your paper.
- Look down at your writing and talk to yourself. Do I have this? Did I do this?
- And compare your writing to the sample posted in that level. Does my writing look like this?
- As you go through the criteria skill by skill, model how you executed some skills some of the time — but not every time.
- And each time you discover something is missing, model how to go back to your seat to add or fix it.

After demonstrating how to add, revise, and edit your writing in order to earn THAT level, show students how to look to the NEXT level. Point out the new skills listed and how they tell you what to do in order to earn THAT star.

section_name: Growing Rubric Concept and Key Takeaways
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly PK-2 Writing Rubrics — Growing Rubric and Key Takeaways

End this second mini-lesson acknowledging that "the Class Writing Rubric is done... for now. We will be adding more NEW skills as they learn more this year." (The process for growing the rubric is revealed within Episode 7 of this TEACH Writing PD Mini-Series.)

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the most important takeaways about building instructional rubrics:

1. They CAN be made simple and accessible even for the lowest grade levels.
2. They MUST be student centered, honoring the writers who will be using it.
3. And unlike checklists, rubrics help students identify WHAT they need to do next to improve their own writing.

So I encourage you to create the wall space, determine the criteria, and make parallel examples in order to generate a Class Writing Rubric. By empowering your young writers to use a kid-friendly writing rubric, we take the next step toward building better writers.
